title: React.js and Next.js
description: Build modern, component-driven user interfaces with React, then ship production-grade applications with Next.js routing, data fetching, and rendering strategies.
objectives: Compose reusable components with props, state, and effects
Manage complex state and side effects with hooks
Fetch, cache, and render data responsibly
Structure a Next.js app with file-based routing
Choose the right rendering strategy for a page

modules.title: React Fundamentals
modules.description: Think in components: JSX, rendering, props, and the component lifecycle.
modules.completionCriteria: Build a static component tree that renders structured data from props without errors.

lessons.title: Thinking in Components
objectives: Explain why UIs are split into components
Identify component boundaries in an existing page

content.introduction: React's core idea is simple: break a screen into small, self-contained functions that each return a piece of UI. Each component owns a slice of the page and can be reused anywhere.
content.explanation: A React component is a function that returns JSX (a syntax extension that looks like HTML). React calls your function with a set of props and renders the result. Because components are plain functions, they compose naturally: a Header can contain a Logo and a Nav, and none of them needs to know how the others work. This isolation is what makes large interfaces maintainable — you change one component without reasoning about the entire page.

examples.title: A simple component
examples.walkthrough: Greeting takes a name prop and returns JSX. App reuses it twice with different data — no duplication, no shared global state.

content.useCase: Navigation bars, product cards, and form fields are classic component boundaries: they appear in multiple places with different data.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a React component?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Components are functions that return JSX; React renders their output.

knowledgeCheck.question: How is data passed into a component?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Props are the read-only inputs a parent passes to a child.

content.summary: Components are reusable functions returning JSX. Props carry data in; composition builds complex UIs from simple parts.

lessons.title: JSX and Rendering
objectives: Explain what React renders and when

content.introduction: JSX lets you describe UI markup inside JavaScript. It compiles to regular function calls, so it follows JavaScript rules — not HTML rules.
content.explanation: JSX expressions must have exactly one root element. Attributes use camelCase (className instead of class, tabIndex instead of tabindex), and you embed JavaScript with curly braces. Babel transforms JSX into React.createElement calls, which React turns into a lightweight description of the UI — an object called a React element. React then reconciles that description with what's currently on screen and applies only the necessary DOM changes.

examples.title: JSX with expressions
examples.walkthrough: Curly braces embed JS. The && operator conditionally renders the admin label. className replaces the HTML class attribute.

content.useCase: Rendering lists, conditional badges, and formatted dates directly in markup.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which JSX attribute sets an HTML class?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: class is a reserved word in JavaScript, so React uses className.

knowledgeCheck.question: How many root elements may a JSX expression have?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A single root keeps the returned tree unambiguous; wrap siblings in a fragment if needed.

content.summary: JSX compiles to element descriptions. One root element, camelCase attributes, curly braces for JavaScript.

content.introduction: Props are a component's contract: the inputs it accepts and the shape it expects.
content.explanation: Props are read-only — a component never mutates its own props. You can destructure them in the signature, supply defaults with parameter defaults, and pass arbitrary nested markup through the special children prop. Callback props let children notify parents, which is how state flows downward and events flow upward in React's unidirectional data model.

examples.title: Defaults, children, and callbacks
examples.walkthrough: variant defaults to primary, children overrides label when present, and onDelete lets the parent handle the click.

content.useCase: Design systems where a single Button component serves every screen via props.

knowledgeCheck.question: Can a component modify the props it receives?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Mutating props breaks React's data-flow assumptions; derive new values instead.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the children prop contain?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: children captures whatever you nest inside the component's tags.

content.summary: Props are read-only inputs with defaults and children. Callback props carry events back up to the parent.

lessons.title: Choosing Component Boundaries
objectives: Split a page into components by responsibility

content.introduction: Good boundaries make code reusable; bad ones create coupling. The goal is to split by responsibility, not by size.
content.explanation: A useful rule: extract a component when it has its own meaningful name in your product vocabulary — ProductCard, SearchBar, InvoiceTotal. Split further when a piece has independent state or props that change for unrelated reasons. Avoid extracting too early: duplicating three lines twice is cheaper than inventing the wrong abstraction. When a component needs more than a handful of props, it is usually doing too much.

examples.title: Before and after
examples.walkthrough: Each child has a single job and its own props, so any of them can change or be reused independently.

content.useCase: Any dashboard or marketing page that mixes several distinct regions.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the best signal that something should be its own component?
options: It has a meaningful name and independent responsibilities
It appears twice in the same file
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Named responsibilities predict where changes will happen; length alone does not.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is premature abstraction?
options: Building a reusable piece before its requirements are clear
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The wrong shared component is more expensive than temporary duplication.

content.summary: Split by named responsibility and independent state. Duplicate small amounts until the pattern is obvious.

modules.title: State and Events
modules.description: Make components interactive with state, event handlers, and controlled inputs.
modules.completionCriteria: Build an interactive form that validates input and updates UI from state.

content.introduction: State is data that changes over time and causes the UI to update when it does.
content.explanation: useState returns the current value and a setter. Calling the setter schedules a re-render of that component (and its children). Two things surprise beginners: React batches updates so multiple setters in one handler produce a single render, and the setter ignores changes when the new value is identical to the current one (Object.is comparison) — so always compute from the previous value when updating based on it.

examples.title: Counter with functional update
examples.walkthrough: The functional form (c) => c + 1 always sees the latest value, even across batched updates.

content.useCase: Counters, toggles, expand/collapse panels, and any UI that remembers something between renders.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does calling a useState setter do?
options: Schedules a re-render of the component
knowledgeCheck.explanation: React re-renders and diffs the output to update only what changed.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why use the functional updater form setCount(c => c + 1)?
options: It reads the latest state even when updates are batched
It is faster in every case
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Batching can defer the new value; the functional form receives the pending value.

content.summary: State drives re-renders. Use functional updaters when new state depends on the old.

lessons.title: Handling Events
objectives: Understand event pooling and synthetic events

content.introduction: React wraps native events in synthetic events with a consistent API across browsers.
content.explanation: Event handlers are passed as functions — onClick, onChange, onSubmit — and receive a synthetic event object. Because handlers are closures, they capture the values from the render they were created in; if a handler needs a fresh value, include it in the dependency array of a callback or read it from state. React attaches listeners at the root, which makes event handling efficient and consistent.

examples.title: Handler with captured values
examples.walkthrough: The inline arrow captures item.id at render time, so the parent receives the right identifier.

content.useCase: Any interactive control: buttons, list actions, drag handles, keyboard shortcuts.

knowledgeCheck.question: How does React receive native events?
options: Through synthetic events attached at the root
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Root delegation gives consistent behavior and one listener per event type.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why might an inline handler see stale values?
options: Closures capture the render they were created in
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Include the value in state or a ref if the handler must read the latest.

content.summary: Handlers are closures over their render. Use synthetic events for cross-browser consistency.

content.introduction: A controlled input's value comes from state, making React the single source of truth.
content.explanation: Set value from state and update it in onChange. This lets you validate as the user types, enforce formatting (uppercasing a code field), disable submit until the form is valid, and reset the form in one place. On submit, read the state values rather than scraping the DOM. Because React controls the value, you can never end up with an input showing something state does not know about.

examples.title: Validated form
examples.walkthrough: value + onChange keep state in sync; validation runs before submit; the button disables until there is input.

content.useCase: Search boxes with debounce, checkout forms, profile editors, and any input needing instant feedback.

knowledgeCheck.question: What makes an input 'controlled'?
options: Its value is set from React state
knowledgeCheck.explanation: value comes from state and onChange writes back to it.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why call e.preventDefault() in a form submit handler?
options: To stop the browser's default full-page navigation
knowledgeCheck.explanation: React apps handle submission in JS; the default would reload the page.

content.summary: Bind value to state, update on change, validate before submit. React stays the single source of truth.

modules.title: Hooks in Depth
modules.description: Effects, context, and custom hooks for logic that outlives a single component.
modules.completionCriteria: Implement an effect with correct cleanup and extract a reusable custom hook.

content.introduction: Effects synchronize React with things outside it: networks, subscriptions, timers, and the DOM.
content.explanation: By default an effect runs after every commit. A dependency array narrows that to only when listed values change; an empty array runs once after mount. Anything an effect creates — timers, listeners, subscriptions — must be torn down in the returned cleanup function, which runs before the next effect and on unmount. Think of an effect as a contract: whatever you set up, you take down.

examples.title: Subscription with cleanup
examples.walkthrough: The effect registers a listener; the returned function removes it. Running the effect once keeps a single listener alive.

content.useCase: Subscribing to WebSocket feeds, media queries, and browser events from a hook.

knowledgeCheck.question: When does a useEffect with [] run?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An empty dependency array limits the effect to mount.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of the function returned from useEffect?
options: Cleanup — it runs before the next effect and on unmount
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cleanup prevents leaked listeners, timers, and subscriptions.

content.summary: Effects sync with the outside world. Declare dependencies honestly and always clean up.

content.introduction: Context passes data through intermediate components without threading props at every level.
content.explanation: Create a context, wrap a subtree in its Provider with a value, and read it from any descendant with the useContext hook. This suits genuinely global data — theme, authenticated user, locale. It is a poor fit for fast-changing values consumed by few components, because every consumer re-renders whenever the value changes; keep the value stable (useMemo) or split contexts by concern.

examples.title: Theme context
examples.walkthrough: Toolbar reads context directly; no intermediate component forwards anything. useMemo keeps the value reference stable.

content.useCase: Theme, auth session, feature flags, and locale shared across an entire app.

knowledgeCheck.question: What problem does context solve?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It provides a direct channel to deep descendants.

knowledgeCheck.question: What happens when a context value changes?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Keep the value small or memoized to limit re-renders.

content.summary: Context eliminates prop drilling for genuinely shared data. Stabilize the value to avoid excess renders.

content.introduction: Custom hooks package stateful logic so multiple components can share it without sharing state.
content.explanation: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that may call other hooks. Extract one when two components duplicate the same state-and-effect pattern — a fetch with loading and error, a media-query subscription, an interval. The rules of hooks still apply: call hooks unconditionally at the top level, never in loops or branches. Each call of the hook keeps its own independent state.

examples.title: A fetch hook
examples.walkthrough: The hook owns the whole lifecycle, cancels in-flight requests on cleanup, and returns a consistent shape.

content.useCase: Shared data fetching, keyboard shortcuts, viewport detection, and debounce logic.

knowledgeCheck.question: What naming convention marks a custom hook?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The use prefix lets React's linter enforce the rules of hooks.

knowledgeCheck.question: Can two components using the same custom hook share state?
options: No, each call keeps its own state
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Hooks return values, not shared storage; each invocation is independent.

content.summary: Custom hooks share logic, not state. Follow the rules of hooks and keep them focused.

modules.title: Next.js for Production
modules.description: File-based routing, data fetching, and choosing how each page renders.
modules.completionCriteria: Scaffold a Next.js app with dynamic routes and an appropriate rendering strategy per page.

content.introduction: In the Next.js App Router, the folder structure under app/ defines the URL structure.
content.explanation: Each folder is a route segment; page.jsx inside it defines the UI at that URL. Dynamic segments use bracket syntax — [id] captures one segment, [...slug] captures any number. Because routing happens on the server, you can read params directly in a server component and fetch exactly the data that route needs, with no client-side router configuration.

examples.title: Dynamic route
examples.walkthrough: params is awaited, data is fetched on the server, and a missing record triggers the not-found boundary.

content.useCase: Job detail pages, blog posts, and user profiles — anything keyed by an id in the URL.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does a folder named [id] under app/ create?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The bracket makes the segment a parameter that varies per URL.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does [...slug] match?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A catch-all captures nested paths under its parent route.

content.summary: Folders become routes; brackets create dynamic and catch-all segments.

lessons.title: Choosing a Rendering Strategy
objectives: Compare SSR, SSG, and client rendering

content.introduction: Different pages have different freshness and performance needs — Next.js lets you choose per route.
content.explanation: Static generation builds the HTML once at deploy time: fastest and cheapest, ideal for content that rarely changes. Server rendering generates HTML per request: always fresh, ideal for personalized or rapidly changing data. Client-side rendering hydrates in the browser: best for highly interactive views where initial HTML matters less. The right choice is a product decision — freshness versus speed — not a default you apply everywhere.

examples.title: Per-page decisions
examples.walkthrough: Each route declares its own freshness contract; static pages can revalidate on an interval.

content.useCase: Blog posts static, dashboards dynamic, editors client-side — one app, three strategies.

knowledgeCheck.question: When is static generation the best choice?
options: Content that rarely changes and must load fast
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Static HTML is the fastest option and trivially cacheable.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does force-dynamic do?
options: Renders the page on every request
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Use it when the response must reflect the latest data.

content.summary: Match the strategy to freshness needs: static for stable content, dynamic for live data, client for rich interaction.

content.introduction: Server components can await data directly, which removes client-side fetch boilerplate.
content.explanation: In an async server component, await your data source and render it — no useEffect, no loading flag, no waterfall. For perceived performance, wrap slow sections in Suspense with a fallback so the rest of the page streams immediately. Errors belong in error boundaries, which keep a broken widget from taking down the whole route. Reserve client-side fetching for data that genuinely depends on browser state or user interaction.

examples.title: Streaming with Suspense
examples.walkthrough: Header paints instantly; the slow section streams in behind a skeleton without blocking the route.

content.useCase: Dashboards with one slow widget, product pages with personalized carousels.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why await data in a server component instead of useEffect?
options: No client bundle cost and no loading-state boilerplate
It is the only valid way
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The data never needs to cross the network to the browser.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does Suspense's fallback render?
options: Placeholder UI while the section loads
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It gives users immediate feedback instead of a blank region.

content.summary: Fetch on the server, stream slow parts with Suspense, and contain failures with error boundaries.
